To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
B cells from RA‐synovium show hypermutation and affinity maturation for IgVH as well as for IgVL/λ, and that this is not related to rheumatoid factor production.

B cell hybridomas derived from the synovial membrane of patients with RA are negative for RF but positive for mutated IgVH, IgVL and λ genes, indicating an antigen‐drived selection of the synovial B cell repertoire.

“Molecular analysis of B cell hybridomas derived from rheumatoid tissue revealed an antigen‐drived process, with selection of high‐mutated IgVH genes, and low‐mutated IgVL/λ, which are negative for rheumatoid factor.”
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular and cellular mechanisms of the local B cell response in synovial tissues and its possible role in the pathogenesis of RA.

the molecular analysis of the synovial B cell population in patients with RA, which may be important for the understanding of the local B cell proliferation and for the development of new therapeutic strategies.
a novel concept of the pathogenesis of RA, which is based on the local antigen‐induced selection of mutated RF‐negative B cells in the synovium.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
in the synovitis of the affected joints of patients with RA an antigen‐dependent stimulation and selection of mutated Ig genes occurs, which is independent of the production of RF.
RF‐negative synovial tissue‐derived B cell hybridomas are stimulated by antigens other than RF, and that these hybridomas are selected for high mutated VH and low mutated VL/λ genes.
the synovial B cell expansion and the local chronic inflammation in RA is driven by antigen(s) other than RF, but RF is involved in the pathogenesis and in the systemic symptoms of RA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the synovium in RA is an active site for antigen‐dependent B cell expansion, and that RF is only one of several antigens that can be involved in the pathogenesis of RA.
the synovial B cell expansion of RA is antigen‐driven and is not related to RF, but to other antigens.
antigen stimulation and selection for mutated IgVH genes is a common feature of B cells in the synovium of RA patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
B cell hybridomas derived from synovial membrane without prior in vitro selection show evidence of somatic hypermutation of the immunoglobulin variable genes and affinity selection.
B cell hybridomas can be produced from rheumatoid arthritis synovial tissue and these cells can be used as a model to investigate the pathogenesis of RA.
the synovial B‐cell expansion is antigen‐driven.
